opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's one of those dynamics that hasn't gotten as much attention as it deserves. A lot of the classic discussion of discontinuous progress was about the underlying capability itself: does some algorithmic insight suddenly make a system vastly smarter overnight? At AI Impacts we've spent a lot of time looking at historical technology trends and asking how often you actually see big jumps, and the answer is: not that often, though more often than zero.

But there's a different route to something that looks discontinuous from the outside, even if the underlying models are improving fairly smoothly. Over time, we're building up a huge amount of scaffolding around these systems: tool integrations, agent frameworks, APIs wired into businesses, workflows that assume a model sits in a certain slot. All of that infrastructure gets built with the current generation of models in mind, and it's sort of waiting there. Then a new model comes along that's somewhat better, maybe crosses some reliability threshold, and you can drop it into all of that existing plumbing basically instantly. So the effective impact in the world could jump a lot even if the benchmark improvement was modest.

It's a bit like having a lot of slack in the system. If the model was the bottleneck, and everything else is already in place, then relieving the bottleneck releases a lot at once. That's quite different from the historical pattern where a new technology arrives and then you spend years or decades building the complementary infrastructure before it really matters.

So the reason I'd want to ask researchers about it is partly that I genuinely don't know how seriously people take it. Do the people building these systems think this kind of overhang is real and large? Do they expect it to produce sudden shifts in what AI is doing in the economy, or in how much autonomy these systems effectively have? And it matters for things like how much warning we get. If the picture is "capabilities creep up and society adjusts," that's one world. If it's "capabilities creep up, and deployment lurches forward in steps," then policy and safety work have to be ready ahead of the step rather than reacting to it.

And surveys are useful for exactly this kind of thing: it's not that the researchers are oracles, but if there's a broad sense among people close to the work that this is plausible, that's informative, and if there's a big disagreement, that's informative too.

r001.rationale: The response cites uncertainty about whether researchers and people close to the work consider infrastructure overhang plausible, but it does not identify policy-adjacent thought leaders as the group whose uncertainty motivates the survey question.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it merits a question because it's a scenario where the thing that would be surprising isn't really progress in the models themselves, it's how much of the world is already set up to absorb them. A lot of the debate about discontinuity has focused on whether capabilities jump, whether you get some sudden leap in what a model can do. But there's a separate question, which is: even if capabilities improve fairly smoothly, could the impact be discontinuous because there's a lot of infrastructure already sitting there waiting, and at some threshold a model becomes good enough to plug into it?

So you can imagine all these existing systems, software pipelines, APIs, robotics platforms, financial systems, scientific workflows, that were built for humans or for narrower tools, and they're kind of latent capacity. A model that's slightly better than the last one might cross from "not quite reliable enough to be trusted in that pipeline" to "reliable enough," and then suddenly it's deployed everywhere at once, because the deployment cost is close to zero. That's a very different dynamic from historical technologies, where you usually had to build out the complementary infrastructure over years, and that building was itself the bottleneck that smoothed things out.

And the reason I'd want it in the survey specifically is that I don't think I know what researchers believe about this, and I suspect they disagree a lot. When we've asked about discontinuity in the past, people have mostly interpreted it as a question about algorithms or compute. I'd like to separate those out, because the policy implications are quite different. If you think the main risk of sudden change comes from capability jumps, you watch the labs and the benchmarks. If you think it comes from infrastructure absorption, you'd want to be watching things like how many systems have standardized interfaces that an AI could step into, how much decision-making authority is already delegated to automated processes, that sort of thing.

I'd also say there's a kind of epistemic humility reason. Our surveys have historically been useful partly because they capture things the community turned out to be wrong about, or divided on, and this feels like a place where intuitions are strong and poorly examined. People who work on deployment often seem to think it's obvious that integration is slow and messy and full of friction, and people who think about the strategic picture often seem to assume the opposite. Getting a distribution of views on the record, with some specificity about mechanism, seems more valuable than another round of asking when human-level AI will arrive.

r001.rationale: The response says the speaker does not know what researchers believe and suspects they disagree, but it does not identify uncertainty among policy-adjacent thought leaders as the reason for including the question.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a distinction between how smoothly the models themselves improve and how smoothly their effects on the world increase. You could have fairly continuous progress in model capabilities, but then cross a threshold where a model can do a useful job within infrastructure that already exists. At that point, you might be able to deploy it very widely without first having to build a whole new system around it.

That doesn’t necessarily imply a discontinuity. There could be all sorts of bottlenecks—reliability, integration, people being willing to use it. But it seems like a plausible mechanism for relatively abrupt change that a question about the pace of model improvement might miss.

So I’d be interested in asking researchers whether they expect that kind of threshold, and what they think would constrain deployment once you cross it. Otherwise, we might hear that they expect gradual progress and interpret that as gradual change in the world, when those are actually different claims.

r001.rationale: The response explains why infrastructure could enable abrupt real-world change and says researchers should be asked about it, but it does not cite uncertainty among policy-adjacent thought leaders as a reason for including the question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a question of whether progress in the models themselves is the right thing to be looking at. You could have fairly continuous improvements in AI capabilities, but then reach a point where a model is good enough to slot into some existing system, and suddenly you can do a lot more with it. You don’t have to build all the complementary infrastructure from scratch—it’s already there.

For instance, if an AI becomes able to do a particular job, there may already be computers and communication systems and organizations through which you could deploy many copies of it. So the change in what’s happening in the world could be much more abrupt than the change in the underlying model.

I’m uncertain how important that effect is, and I’d be interested in whether researchers expect it. Asking about it separately could help distinguish expectations about smooth capability improvements from expectations about how smoothly those improvements translate into economic activity or other consequential outcomes.

r001.rationale: The response says the speaker is uncertain how important the effect is and wants to know whether researchers expect it, but does not cite uncertainty among policy-adjacent thought leaders.
